We develop a novel local constant fitting algorithm and establish its optimal convergence rate under the Frobenius norm. This approach yields a nonparametric time-varying estimator for the Poisson coefficient function, which can be further extended to a nonconstant estimator that accounts for potential periodicity. Theoretical analysis reveals that this estimator converges to the underlying true parameter at an optimal rate. Practical applications are demonstrated through a word count dataset and an analysis of the impact of external covariates on data patterns, highlighting the model's ability to identify structural breaks and nonlinear relationships. Additionally, the nonparametric time-varying estimator uncovers interesting features regarding the nonlinear dynamics of the word count data. To facilitate usage, we have made the R package "tvparx" available at https://github.com/wenqianqiu/tvparx. Our work contributes to the literature by proposing a time-varying Poisson model with external covariates, developing a local constant fitting method, deriving optimal convergence rates for both parametric and nonparametric estimators (including time-varying coefficient estimators), and validating these findings through real-world applications. This study presents a method for determining the vertical aerosol optical depth ($\tau$) via wide-field photometry, eliminating the need for absolute calibration. This approach builds upon the technique outlined by Gai et al. (2020), who utilized a coronameter to monitor fluctuations in a small, local patch of sky brightness. In contrast, this work employs public surveys from the ZWI and OMEGA wide-field photometers to analyze brightness variations across extensive areas of the sky. These variations result from changes in the atmospheric path length, which are controlled by a simple linear model incorporating the zenith angle and horizontal wind speed and direction. The data were collected at the 1.52-m telescope of the University of Chile's Robotic Telescopes Network in Cerro Pachon (latitude -30.4, longitude -70.7). Results indicate that this method achieves a precision of 0.005 for $\tau$ (equivalent to 0.32 Angstroms at 550 nm), maintaining linearity even under highly turbulent conditions where $\tau$ reaches 0.2. Although this technique functions as a relative radiometer and cannot replace absolute calibration standards, it offers rapid, real-time verification of calibration stability. Furthermore, its simplicity, speed, and ability to operate unattended make it an excellent complement to spectroscopic instruments, ensuring optimal utilization of precious observing time. The source code for this package is accessible at https://github.com/UCHilettecs/UCHNRAO_AirMass. Instrumental photometric points from the ZWI and OMEGA telescopes, along with derived atmospheric parameters, are accessible through the UCHETE public database at http://db.uche.te/ or the ApED portal at http://aped.harvard.edu/. Additionally, this simple model may find applications in other contexts, such as correcting for atmospheric extinction in galaxyanemone red curve measurements or serving as a "smog meter" for meteorological monitoring.
This study evaluates the computational efficiency and accuracy of a newly implemented multiconfigurational time-dependent Hartree (MCTDH) approach for simulating biomolecular systems, using the alanine dipeptide as a model. We compare MCTDH with density functional theory (TD-DFT) and conventional wavefunction theory (CT-WFT), focusing on a reactive simulation involving proton transfer between amino and ammonium groups. The framework employs a mixed continuous-discrete representation, applying tensor optimization for discrete coordinates and time-dependent mode optimization for continuous ones. Results indicate that the efficiency gains from MCTDH over CT-WFT are substantial, scaling linearly with the number of discrete coordinates and nearly linearly with their size. Furthermore, for the specific reactions modeled here, the accuracy of the optimized discrete grid and continuous wavefunction surpasses that of the numerical grid used in CT-WFT. These findings suggest that MCTDH offers both significant computational advantages and enhanced accuracy regarding coordinates of interest compared to CT-WFT, making it a potent tool for investigating reaction dynamics in biomolecules. Additional coordinate systems and reactions will be explored in future work. As a testament to the method's efficiency and flexibility, we present records of simulations with ten binary coordinates and a system comprising 69 atoms, for which no exact treatment of reaction dynamics has been achieved previously. To maximize computational resource utilization, we detail strategies for parallelizing the MCTDH code across multiple CPUs and utilizing GPU acceleration. All source code, configurations for published examples, and a user guide are accessible via https://github.com/alexei-meyer/B96-MCTDH. Notably, the code's flexibility allows for the simulation of any many-body quantum system, regardless of whether it is a small molecule like the alanine dipeptide or a larger collection of atoms, by appropriately defining coordinates and boundary conditions. Additionally, it can handle systems where the "exact" quantum treatment of all degrees of freedom is currently infeasible, such as conventional molecular dynamics simulations involving thousands of atoms. Finally, we demonstrate that the mixed continuous-discrete coordinate system can effectively model systems with both discrete and continuous spatial degrees of freedom, including rotational states, vibrational excitations, electronic states, and nuclear positions.
While the majority of image captioning systems achieve high scores on existing English-dataset benchmarks, these datasets were created by a single group and lack the diverse, high-quality guidelines necessary for visually impaired users to effectively utilize the resulting descriptions. This single-source variability limits the practical utility of generated captions for this demographic. Consequently, there is an urgent need for a comprehensive framework to establish more robust image description guidelines with greater precision and clarity. This paper introduces a unified framework defining a robust framework for image description generation, offering specific recommendations for both the structural format of descriptions and the semantic level of vocabulary choice. Additionally, we curate a large-scale, multi-format dataset of guidelines—potentially useful as a benchmark—using crowdsourced methods, which we release publicly. Finally, we evaluate multiple existing models against this new dataset to demonstrate the proposed framework's validity and utility. The guidelines outlined in this work are available as a public resource at http://guidelines.id-dataset.org/.

This report offers a comprehensive overview of how Euler-Arnold equations are applied to the definition of the running coupling constant within the Scharfenberg-Orsay (SCO) variant of gravity-borns quantum chromodynamics (QCD). We present novel Euler-Arnold equations tailored for the running coupling in the SCO-QED model, and we detail the numerical strategies employed to solve these equations and optimize the running coupling parameter $\beta_0$. Finally, we compare the optimized running coupling in both SCO-QED and SCO-QCD against the conventional $\overline{MS}$ coupling, providing examples of the resulting benefits. An open-source Python package implementing the methods discussed here is available at https://github.com/utphys582/RunningCoupIng. The pursuit of a quantitative theory of strong interactions relies heavily on the running coupling constant in spectroscopy and numerical simulations, warranting continued research into its definition and characterization. Such efforts yield significant advantages, most notably the increased precision required for the "N-nth" order loop calculations now feasible thanks to computational advances and the optimization of the running coupling. The short-distance nature of the running coupling in SCO-QCD should facilitate its application to massive quantum fields, potentially serving as a viable alternative to $\overline{MS}$ for large spacelike momenta in near-future numerical studies. Additionally, the optimized running coupling in SCO-QCD may find uses in other areas of quantum field theory. Notably, the direct, short-distance definition of the running coupling in SCO-QCD should enable a straightforward determination of its value at the $Z$-boson mass, helping resolve discrepancies between lattice QCD results and those derived from neutral-current weak interactions at the LHC. Furthermore, similar to spectroscopy, the direct characterization of strong interactions at large spacelike momenta in meson form factors should prove beneficial. Because the running coupling in SCO-QCD is defined non-perturbatively at large spacelike momenta (unlike in $\overline{MS}$, where it is extrapolated from the $Z$-boson mass), it should eliminate artifact discrepancies between calculations performed at different momentum scales. Finally, this work should assist in clarifying misconceptions regarding the running coupling in quantum field theory; for instance, it is erroneous to claim that the running coupling "vanishes" at large distances
The interaction of heavy quarks in QCD is analogous to that of any two particles, with the resulting bound states termed heavy quarkonia. These states function as probes for new physics, serving much like an atomic spectrometer does in atomic physics. In this introduction to a non-trivial subject, we present the leading-order (LO) and next-to-leading-order (NLO) QCD corrections governing the production of heavy quarkonia from initial-state mesons. We begin by outlining the production mechanism, which comprises three distinct vertices: a vertex creating the pair of heavy quarks, a vertex emitting a gluon that forms a quarkonium vertex, and finally the vertex where the heavy quarkonium is produced. We then detail the calculation of the three possible LO diagrams and their corresponding NLO contributions. The LO processes involve emitting a gluon to form quarkonium at two vertices and fusing with an incoming gluon to create the quarkonium at a third vertex. Our calculation of LO and NLO processes includes real emission and virtual correction diagrams. Following the calculation, we display the differential cross-section for producing a $\\eta_c$ at leading order and its dependence on transverse momentum. We also examine the impact of varying renormalization and factorization scales. Finally, utilizing the MadGraph5_a@v code, we calculate the differential cross-section for $\\eta_c$ production with transverse momentum dependence, comparing results across different parton shower implementations. Our findings indicate that the ratio of NLO to LO cross-sections remains constant when varying transverse momentum. Furthermore, the dependence on parton showers is evident in the differential cross-section as a function of $p_T$, with the MadEvent calculation yielding a higher cross-section than the MadGraph5_a@v result.
This study investigates the fair-throughput and sum-throughput optimization challenges addressed by a wideband waveforming (WBWF) system for multiple users (MUs) communicating with a single cognitive base station (CBS). Capacity for every MU is formulated as the maximum quantity of an encoded RB accessible within its specific IWB range. Depending on the total available RBs, two distinct wideband access schemes are considered: a single-MU access scheme, where only one MU utilizes the WBRF, and a multi-MU access scheme, enabling multiple MUs to use the RB simultaneously via spatial division multiple access (SDMA). The fair-throughput and sum-throughput optimization problems are modeled for both access schemes. These issues are solved using a step-by-step algorithm, comparing fair-throughput constraints across the single-MU and multi-MU schemes to determine the optimal allocation. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that the proposed optimization framework significantly enhances both fair-throughput and sum-throughput compared to various threshold-based and random allocation strategies. Furthermore, the study confirms that increasing the total number of available IWB Rs and the maximum supportable RB count substantially improves both fair-throughput and sum-throughput. Ultimately, this work offers a useful reference for optimizing communications among MUs and a single CBS.

We observe that the constitutive relation of nonlocal gravity proposed by Gorgham, Kummer, and Sievers (GKSS) -- which links the tensor of extra curvature to traces of the mass -- is not directly observable. In contrast, the constitutive relation adopted by nonlocal models of biophysics and materials science connects an unknown field to an observable quantity. Guided by this distinction, we modify the nonlocal gravitational model of GKSS by replacing their constitutive relation with a new, observable-based relation that remains general. Consequently, the field equations become integro-differential equations involving both the Einstein tensor and the new constitutive relation. To assess whether this revised model offers a superior fit to cosmological data compared to $\Lambda$CDP, we utilize two distinct formulations for the unknown constitutive relation: a single-fluid model and a two-fluid model. Analysis of the single-fluid model indicates it performs poorly relative to $\Lambda$CDP when constrained by both cosmological and local observations. The single-fluid results suggest a constitutive relation composed of a combination of single- and double-curvature tensors may be superior; therefore, we examine the two-fluid model. Fitting this model to cosmological data alone yields results similar to the two-elastic-strain relation in biophysics/materials science, which are notably different from both $\Lambda$CDP and the single-fluid model. However, incorporating local observations causes the two-fluid model to degrade significantly, failing to match cosmological data as effectively as the single-fluid approach. Ultimately, we conclude that a constitutive relation analogous to those in biophysical/materials science is incompatible with local gravitational measurements. Furthermore, we find that cosmic structures act as a potent probe for physics beyond $\Lambda$CDP, potentially serving as a future detection method for nonlocal gravitational effects. Finally, this study underscores the necessity of establishing an explicit constitutive relation rooted in observables for nonlocal theories of gravity.

The observation of an accretion-powered millisecond radio pulsar represents a crucial step toward understanding the complete millisecond neutron star population in the Galaxy and the associated evolutionary channels. Given that many of these systems are likely to convert from X-ray to radio emission, we project that approximately 20 neutron star low mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) should be seen in the sensitive band of the new eRGO telescope. These systems would constitute millisecond LMXBs, which are expected to exhibit intrinsic luminosities comparable to typical variable LMXBs and exhibit masses for the companion star similar to those found in radio millisecond pulsar systems. These millisecond LMXBs would also display the characteristic clustering in pulse fraction and spin period observed in neutron star recollapsing high mass X-ray binaries. While the actual detection of such systems will depend on the ultimate sensitivity of eRGO and its observation time, their existence would imply a population of millisecond neutron stars that is as abundant as the millisecond radio pulsar population in the Galaxy.
We introduce a technique for a bipartite graph that enables near-optimal vertex splitting to yield a planar embedding accounting for all original-edge adjacencies. This approach yields a bipartite drawing with at most one curved edge per vertex and achieves linear area efficiency. Consequently, we present an algorithm that splits vertices to produce a planar visualization maintaining linear area efficiency and preserving the adjacency of nearly all original vertices (specifically, all but one). Combining our methods, we deliver a linear-time algorithm for any bipartite graph that generates a planar drawing with at most one curved edge per vertex and linear area efficiency, retaining the adjacency of all but one vertex (potentially the one with the highest degree). Furthermore, we extend this solution to general graphs, resulting in an algorithm capable of creating planar drawings that preserve adjacency for almost every vertex while ensuring linear area efficiency. Our findings demonstrate that preserving almost all vertex adjacencies and maintaining linear area efficiency are both achievable even when the graph is fully connected. Additionally, we provide an algorithm preserving almost all edge adjacencies with linear area efficiency that incorporates a small set of excluded adjacencies, possibly including the adjacency between two specific vertices. To illustrate the limitations of adjacency preservation under linear area constraints, we also include negative results regarding the simultaneous preservation of almost all vertex and edge adjacencies. Finally, we apply our methods to real-world networks, splitting a limited number of vertices to generate planar visuals with linear area efficiency and high adjacency accuracy. Our experiments confirm that linear area efficiency remains viable for large-scale real-world networks, and the visualizations effectively highlight which vertex adjacencies are not represented due to space limitations. Regarding positive results, we detail an algorithm that utilizes all available area to maximize adjacency preservation, accompanied by a real-world network example demonstrating its outcomes. For negative insights, we address the challenge of minimizing curved edges in bipartite graphs, presenting an asymptotically optimal lower bound and an construction matching this bound; however, we admit open challenges related to achieving linearity in this specific context.

This research investigates how the distribution of activity difficulties influences the multi-agent dynamics of a simple task-based game. We define a stochastic model where an agent team must resolve a fixed number of tasks varying in difficulty, with each agent capable of handling one task at a time and success probabilities dependent on both the task's difficulty and the specific agent assigned. The objective function is based on the residuals of the total work completed within a limited time frame. Although the exact optimization of this criterion for a finite horizon is an NP-hard problem, we apply a greedy decision-theoretic approach at each step to select the agent-task assignment. Given that the dynamics are not strictly stochastic but rather depend on past decisions, we develop a novel method to derive a state representation suitable for solving the resulting decision model. Specifically, we propose a distribution centered on a residual-work vector, optimized via a point-process approach. Considering a linear time-invariant (LIT) relationship between decision history and residual work, we derive a linear update law for this distribution, solving the resulting linearly structured Bayesian game over a finite horizon using an ADVP (adaptive dynamic programming) algorithm. We validate the efficacy of this strategy through simulations, particularly regarding changes in task difficulty distribution, and compare it against a uniform task distribution. Additionally, we address an infinite-horizon linear quadratic Gaussian (LQG) game approximation, demonstrating the utility of our framework for constructing data-driven solutions in similar scenarios. Our findings reveal that the distribution of task difficulties significantly impacts the optimal decision-making policy and highlights the importance of considering the residual work distribution in real-time strategic choices. Furthermore, the proposed LIT residual work distribution model proves effective for constructing data-driven LQG solutions.

For instance, such a set constitutes an algebra over a two-element generating set within the variety of right alternative rings. We demonstrate that the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer yields enhanced sensitivity for low amplitudes when operated under optimal mixing conditions, potentially offering greater advantages than conventional interferometric configurations. This increased sensitivity-at-remaining-amplitude could enable the detection of gravitational waves at frequencies previously below the sensor's peak response. Furthermore, this work clarifies why such modes are advantageous for bypassing the quantum back-action limit in standard interferometers. Additionally, we identify a state-of-the-art sensitivity slope for sloshing-Sagnac interferometers at their characteristic frequency, measuring $1.4 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{m}/\text{dB}$, which surpasses the slope achieved by the most sensitive state-of-the-art bowtie interferometer ($7.8 \times 10^{-10} \, \text{m}/\text{dB}$). Our findings provide a foundation for deploying sloshing-Sagnac topologies as a filter-cavity arrangement to further explore the benefits of multi-arm interferometers. These systems hold significant promise for extending the sensitivity of existing gravitational-wave detectors and future installations, ensuring the observation of weak tidal gravitational wave signals induced by intermediate-mass black hole mergers during their final inspiral phase. To facilitate these explorations, we present an open-source Python package, slovagn, designed for the design, simulation, and construction of sloshing-Sagnac interferometers. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/g-waves/slovagn.
Large-scale multiple-access systems, particularly Extra-L scale MIMO (XL-MIMO), are anticipated to be a cornerstone of future 6G networks, offering substantial gains in spectral and energy efficiency. However, the random access (AA) performance in XL-MIMO remains a significant bottleneck, and the challenges in extra-large deployments are even more pronounced. This paper introduces NOVR-XL, a simplified NOVR-based AA protocol tailored for XL-MIMO, and enhances it to create the NOVR-XL PROVR-XL RA protocol. Furthermore, we develop an optimized variant of NOVR-XL termed NOVR-XL RA. Our simulation results demonstrate that the improved PROVR-XL delivers superior AA performance than NOVR-XL across various AA loads and user equipment counts, while scaling more effectively with the system antenna count. These findings indicate that the simplified protocol is particularly beneficial in extra-large deployments. To validate these conclusions, we compare the scaled AA performance between the NOVR-XL / PROVR-XL protocols and the grid-based GRD-RXL protocol, confirming the enhanced performance of our proposed schemes. Ultimately, the NOVR-XL family of protocols emerges as a cost-effective, practical solution for implementing AA in realistic extra-large MIMO systems. To further enhance NOVR-XL performance, we propose DOVR-XL and COVR-XL protocols utilizing orthogonal division methods based OFDM and RADAR, respectively; however, their superior AA performance depends on accurate channel state information (CSI) estimation, which is difficult to achieve in practice due to the massive CSI matrix size. Finally, we conclude by discussing the potential for further improving the NOVR-XL framework.

This paper introduces a novel training framework for these hybrids, utilizing an $N$-gram component trained via a maximum likelihood estimator and a neural component based on a transformer architecture. We evaluate this framework for phrase-based machine translation, comparing results against a standard model using the same neural architecture. On the test set of the full MultiNUT dataset, our method achieved a 0.4-point improvement in BLEOU over the baseline on the德语 (German) target, while the subset test results on IWSLT showed comparable gains. Furthermore, the benefits observed on the smaller IWSLT dataset suggest that these hybrid models are particularly advantageous for low-resource language pairs. Regarding computational efficiency, our approach was approximately 2x faster on the MultiNUT test set than the baseline, and significantly more efficient on the limited-capacity IWSLT test set. This study investigates the formation of baroclinic storms in an Earth-like atmosphere confined to a planet possessing a solid inner core surrounded by a thick, supercritical outer layer. Using a two-layer model comprising the outer envelope and the inner core, we examine equatorially baroclinic instability under varying conditions of specific heat ratio, envelope thickness, and core radius. The resulting most unstable mode exhibits a circulation pattern akin to a Kelvin wave, with rotation direction dependent on latitude; specifically, it mirrors a Mars-confirmed baroclinic storm. Findings indicate that increasing the specific heat ratio, decreasing envelope thickness, and reducing the inner core's radius all lead to an higher growth rate for the most unstable mode, with envelope thickness proving to be the most significant factor. These outcomes offer valuable insights for atmospheric science regarding the potential formation of baroclinic storms on Mars and the gas giant planet HD 209458 b. Additionally, these conclusions suggest applications for astrophysical systems featuring a similar structural configuration.
This paper introduces a new Hankel contour, termed the $H_1$ path, designed for a specific representation of the Gamma function along the negative real axis. We demonstrate that the Gamma function defined via the $H_1$ contour satisfies the fundamental identities, recurrence relations, and Euler's reflection formula. Furthermore, we establish that the Bessel function of the first kind of order zero can be expressed using the $H_1$ path, yielding a formulation equivalent to the standard definition found in literature. Finally, we derive an explicit conversion formula linking the Gamma function representations derived from both the $H_0$ and $H_1$ contours. The detailed proof of this conversion relies on a contour integral involving the product of two Gamma functions, which is evaluated through a residue calculation following a specific change of variables. As an additional contribution, we present a novel integral representation of the Bessel function of the first kind with a general complex order, also based on the $H_1$ path. The significance of this new representation lies in its potential to facilitate proofs regarding the complex differentiability of the Bessel function with respect to its order parameter.
We present a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic approach for simulating short-time quantum correlations within the near-equilibrium regime. This method extends standard hydrodynamics by incorporating a linearized stochastic noise term, offering an alternative to the Belinfante field-theoretic approach for modeling non-equilibrium quantum systems. Unlike traditional methods, our linearized stochastic hydrodynamic (LSH) framework operates as a real-space grid technique that avoids the necessity for fast Fourier transforms, thereby reducing numerical artifacts and enhancing stability. Furthermore, the LSH method requires fewer variables than the Belinfante approach, making it better suited for higher-dimensional systems. When applied to the non-equilibrium quantum gas phase transition, our results align closely with those obtained via the Belinfante method, confirming the validity of linearized stochastic hydrodynamics for systems near equilibrium. Additionally, we introduce an efficient tensor-based solver to accelerate calculations and demonstrate the approach's applicability in large-scale systems. This challenge spurred the rapid creation of numerous proof-of-concept solutions, which now serve as valuable resources for the broader community. We detail the development of a wrapper around this API, which offers a consistent interface for experimental control. Additionally, we provide specific implementations for two prevalent open-source solutions, FORTE and XFORTE, demonstrating how to connect them to the unified API. The proposed solution is entirely software-based and remains neutral regarding the specific experimental setup, requiring only that the setup be controlled via TCP/IP and support basic commands for configuration, execution, and aborting runs. These characteristics make it straightforward to develop additional wrappers for other solutions. Finally, we discuss the benefits and limitations of this approach within the context of the community. Our goal is for this API and its associated wrappers to become a de facto standard, facilitating the rapid deployment of remote access solutions during crises while minimizing the time needed to create new solutions. Ultimately, this standardization allows telework solutions to coexist more effectively with post-pandemic hybrid access models. This paper is a practical work that defines an API and provides concrete examples of its application, rather than focusing on theoretical concepts. This report details the search strategy for neutral long-lived particles (NLSPs) across various decay length ranges ($c\tau$) at colliders with high-energy protons colliding either with protons or ions. The discussion begins with an introduction to NLSPs and their detection methods, followed by a description of the superconducting solenoid (SMOG) apparatus used to measure decay lengths in the c\tau > 1~m regime at proton-proton ($c\tau$~>~1~m) and proton-ion ($c\tau$~>~10~m) colliders for neutral particles with decay lengths between 1~m and 1~km. The report concludes with an overview of upcoming projects aimed at exploring even longer decay lengths. Relevant AMBER, Belle II, LHC, and LHCx experiments are also discussed. As a "missing energy" particle, the NLSP is produced in association with visible decay products of a heavier long-lived particle (LLP). Consequently, the event topology and corresponding search strategies are strongly influenced by the mass ratio between the LLP and the NLSP. Furthermore, the specific decay mode of the LLP and the exact value of the NLSP's decay length ($c\tau$) dictate both the topology of the neutral displacement and the optimal search strategy for that particular mass scale. Therefore, studies of NLSPs over a wide range of mass scales and decay lengths are essential to map out a comprehensive global search strategy. To facilitate this, we present a unified global search strategy for the superconducting solenoid at the SMOG fixed-target experiment, covering mass ratios from 1 to 50 and decay lengths spanning $10^2$~mm to $10^5$~m. We also examine the implications of recent LHC results for the simplified LHC suspended naturalness model. Additionally, we discuss the feasibility of detecting the NLSP at future high-luminosity colliders, including the High Energy Lector (HLC), the High Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC), and the Future Circular Collider (FCC). Finally, we address the stability of the NLSP and its potential for solving the cosmological dark matter problem. By providing a comprehensive review of NLSP searches across multiple collision energies, this report aims to serve as a useful guide for researchers investigating long-lived particles.
We investigated the connection between two methods for detecting lexical changes over time: dictionaries of contextual variance and dictionaries of contextual norm. The assumption underlying lexical change dictionaries based on variance is that a word's usage style has altered, whereas those based on novelty (norm) conclude that new usages have emerged. Using a corpus of Danish news articles spanning a 200-year period, we analyzed 2,000 words selected from a verb-noun grammar framework to compare the outputs of both dictionaries. The findings indicate that both dictionaries often identify the same lexical items as having changed, yet they typically attribute different causes—either a shift in style or the addition of new usages—reflecting a trade-off between variance and norm. Furthermore, we observed that a higher degree of contextual variance within a lexical item's definition increases the likelihood that the other items in its grammatical framework will be classified as changed by the novelty-based dictionary. This suggests that language change can manifest as a reallocation of new usages between words with similar contextual norms, a phenomenon we term the pragmatical spill-over effect. To utilize this phenomenon for identifying morphological or semantic equivalents, we developed a method for constructing a diachronic distributional semantic vector space space from a diachronic corpus. This approach was validated by successfully recovering known historical neologisms and semantic shifts. Finally, we applied this method to a large Danish diachronic corpus to create a distributional semantic vector space, demonstrating its utility in uncovering hidden semantic shifts and enabling the analysis of lexical networks. Our results show that words identified as having changed align significantly more with a list of known semantic shifts derived from etymological dictionaries than words that remain unchanged, an advantage this method holds over traditional contextual variance dictionaries. This measure reveals that focusing solely on corpus frequency can be misleading when seeking words with the greatest potential for new usages, as highly frequent words may already have saturated their contextual contexts. Ultimately, this study underscores the benefit of combining multiple methodologies to comprehensively examine lexical and semantic changes across different layers of language. We observe that for a broad class of strongly driven quantum systems, the expectation value of the temperature operator fails to yield a meaningful result, rendering standard quantum Monte Carlo algorithms ineffective. In contrast, within the high-temperature regime, our findings indicate that the correlation function of the Lindblad damping term remains positive, allowing Gaussian (or more precisely, first-order Petzlandau) states to remain effective for evaluating the path integral. This suggests that Gaussian approaches can be valuable in addressing problems at high temperatures, particularly where Wick decomposition is applicable. Conversely, our analysis demonstrates that coherent states offer no advantages over Gaussian states when dealing with the damping term associated with general non-Greenfunction spectral functions. Furthermore, we clarify misconceptions found in recent literature regarding the application of coherent states to strongly driven systems; such systems are not necessarily found in the regime of high effective "classical" fields, and assuming they occupy coherent states constitutes an unjustified ansatz. Ultimately, we conclude that the validity of utilizing Gaussian and related approximations depends on the specific physical context and the characteristics of the system's spectrum and damping function, rather than solely on the magnitude of driving forces or temperature. We demonstrate that initializing the magnetogram fitting with an explicit magnetic fill fraction estimate—derived from intensity measurements along the pixel's characteristic scale—yields a more accurate final fraction than starting with an arbitrary guess near unity. Ultimately, we find that explicitly accounting for the magnetic fill fraction yields more accurate vector magnetogram fits only when the initial guess is plausible, which is feasible for pixels where the magnetic field direction is nearly vertical. For the majority of pixels in vector magnetograms, explicit and implicit approaches to fill fraction yield comparable results, provided the initial guess in the explicit method is close to one. We conclude that future regularized Tikhonov inversions should trial both explicit and implicit formulations of the fill fraction to determine which produces the most accurate fit for each individual pixel. Similarly, fine-tuning PaLM-E (82B) on reasoning datasets resulted in a 2 percentage point gain in performance. This study investigates a model trained on a massive, manually constructed if-then dataset from the legal domain, covering 1,024 distinct relation types. We address the challenge of if-then relation extraction, which involves defining a function over a hierarchy of relation types, and introduce a unified framework applicable to various neural architectures. The approach entails two phases: first, mapping an if-then pair to a specific type among the 1,024 options, and second, converting this type into a probability distribution across its numerous subtypes via the defined hierarchy. Our results indicate that our hierarchical framework outperforms models using flat relation type sets by a significant margin. Specifically, our model surpasses the prior state-of-the-art by 5.30 F-beta scores and exceeds other neural models by 1-to-3 beta scores. Furthermore, our model demonstrates robustness when trained on a subset of the full dataset and does not underperform relative to models trained on the complete dataset. These findings suggest that neural models benefit from training on the structural hierarchy of if-then types, a conclusion supported by the fact that our model achieves consistent performance whether the number of types is 1024, 500, or 100. To facilitate future research, we publicly release the if-then dataset and our codebase at https://github.com/VirgileFellous/If-Then-RelEx.
This work introduces a learning approach for view synthesis that relies on a structured dual representation. By splitting the function to be learned into task-dependent and task-independent components, we enable the model to extrapolate to novel viewpoints without requiring training samples from those specific views. The core of our method is a dual representation where the primary component captures view-invariant features through a network shared across different viewpoints, and the secondary component describes view-specific characteristics. We validate the efficacy of this framework using two video datasets and two sequences of images. The results on these datasets from a novel viewpoint are nearly as high as the average scores during training. Furthermore, our system outperforms current state-of-the-art methods when faced with videos or images from unseen angles. Our approach is particularly beneficial in scenarios involving first-person perspectives, such as those found in robotics and virtual reality applications.
This study examines the metric dimension of truncated distance spaces, where the geodesic distance in the original graph is capped at a specific threshold to define the truncated space. We introduce a formula for the truncated metric dimension that extends a recent result from [10] regarding the original metric dimension. Additionally, we characterize when the truncated metric dimension adheres to the original geodesic distance and identify the conditions under which the inclusion between truncated and original metric bases is strict. The work also involves investigating the continuity of the truncated metric dimension and determining the exact curve where the metric dimension jumps. Finally, we apply the concepts, results, and techniques developed herein to a biological context.

Fitting differential models to empirical data is a standard method for evaluating the biological plausibility of epidemiological hypotheses and for deriving actionable public health recommendations during crises. However, fitting models without constraining parameters to be biologically feasible can yield unrealistic and misleading forecasts of key epidemiological variables, such as infection rates. This study addresses the challenge of integrating biological feasibility constraints during the fitting process. We introduce a statistical framework that combines ordinary least squares optimization with an active set method to incorporate these constraints. To demonstrate the framework's utility and compare ordinary fitting versus constraint-enabled fitting, we apply differential equation models describing infection dynamics and healthcare system loads in the United States and selected states. The application reveals that ordinary fitting often produces parameter estimates that violate biological feasibility, whereas the new method successfully generates realistic forecasts of epidemiological metrics and reduces errors related to healthcare system capacity predictions. Consequently, this research offers a practical statistical solution for differential model fitting that enhances the biological plausibility of estimated epidemiological variables, thereby increasing the reliability of equation-based models when assessing infection dynamics and healthcare system responses to epidemiological events.

Feasibility-constrained optimization also generates more plausible estimates of biological parameters and produces better fits to the underlying raw data. Consequently, incorporating biological feasibility constraints during the fitting process leads to more realistic estimates of epidemiological variables, improved accuracy in raw data fits, and more reliable public health forecasts and policy recommendations, which is critical during emerging epidemics. The methodological framework presented here is flexible and can be adapted to various differential model forms, data types, and specific biological feasibility requirements.

Multinational enterprises and internet users engage with content across multiple languages, making cross-lingual sentiment analysis—classifying sentiment toward entities in an unknown target language—analytically important. Although numerous studies have addressed English-centric analysis, few solutions exist for other languages. Most existing solutions rely on multitasking models trained on tasks in both source and target languages; however, this requires labeled sentiment data in the target language, which is often unavailable. This work introduces a solution utilizing only labeled data from one or more source languages. We propose a method leveraging multilingual pre-trained language models and domain adaptation techniques, requiring no target-language data. The approach involves three steps: (i) using a pre-trained model, (ii) adapting it via continuous domain adaptation with source-language datasets, and (iii) classifying target-language text through a shared hidden layer without further training. Experiments indicate this method outperforms current state-of-the-art solutions by significant margins across multiple language pairs and datasets. Furthermore, the solution is cost-effective, as it uses a single pre-trained model, and easily deployable for any language pair using an existing English model. Notably, this work represents the first demonstration of continuous domain adaptation for sentiment analysis across language pairs using only source-language datasets. Our methodology and model weights are accessible at https://github.com/abhinav-1998/CrossLingualDomainAdaptation. Additionally, this research employs open-source models and datasets.
We report the detection of a 0.35-cpsec (parts per second) pulsation in the G-type star KIC 9267654, for which we also determine a mass of 1.2 $M_{\odot}$ and a period of 34.8495 $\pm$ 0.0006 D (days). While magnetic braking is the standard mechanism for spinning down low- and intermediate-mass stars during their main-sequence evolution, this effect appears insufficient to account for the star's atypical rotation profile. Plausible additional factors could include strong stellar winds, interactions in a binary system, the loss of angular momentum due to $\alpha$-Centauri-like companions, or the presence of a close-by massive body inducing a similar tidal braking effect. The discovery of this new pulsation and its subsequent characterization will help refine models of fully convective stars and low-mass main-sequence evolution, potentially uncovering further unexpected findings. This study represents the initial identification, characterization, and confirmation of a fully convective star, with a detailed discussion of these implications deferred to a forthcoming publication.
This study introduces MetaFEND, a novel ensemble model designed to strengthen fake news detection on Twitter. The model integrates four distinct classifiers—Gated Recurrent Unit, Long Short-Term Memory, Bidirectional LSTM, and an N-Gram based classifier—whose outputs are combined via a meta-level classifier to produce the final classification. Unlike existing approaches, MetaFEND employs an unsupervised, data-driven method to determine the optimal number of folded ensembles and selects the best ensemble configuration for the meta-level classifier, eliminating the need for a predetermined configuration. The model was evaluated using the competitive IRECIA dataset, demonstrating superior performance over current methods. On this dataset, the F1-score increased by 0.6009, Precision by 0.0501, Recall by 0.0956, and overall accuracy by 0.0221. These findings confirm that MetaFEND effectively identifies various forms of fake news on Twitter, offering a robust solution for combats misinformation. The source code and model are accessible at https://github.com/abdulrhman077/MetaFEND. Additionally, an API for detecting fraudulent content on Twitter is available at https://api.postfactlin.com/RealNewsAPI.

We introduce a new end-to-end framework for partially supervised graphical modeling, designed to leverage both unsupervised feature extraction (SIFT) and supervised feature extraction. We hypothesize that the characteristics identified during the unsupervised phase will benefit the supervised phase for classes present in the labeled data, while the supervised extraction will prioritize discriminative features for those specific classes. To implement this, we integrate a graph neural network (GNN) into the SIFT pipeline to create a graph-based unsupervised extractor (G-SIFT), which utilizes outputs from GNNs for nodes and edges. For the supervised extractor, we replace G-SIFT with a standard supervised network. Before training, the framework is trained independently; the outputs from the unsupervised extractor serve as inputs for the supervised one. For partial labeling, we employ a convex optimization method to determine the decision boundary between classes. For fully supervised learning, this decision boundary is set directly. Experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate that this end-to-end approach significantly outperforms traditional pipelines. Additionally, the proposed method achieves a higher decision boundary accuracy than the state-of-the-art heterogeneous graph neural network method, PartGNN. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/VincentVincent97/ESFNet.
Knowledge graphs (KGs) structured with entity-relation-entity triples are a dominant form of structured data, yet their underutilization in natural language processing (NLP) datasets represents a significant waste of data diversity. This paper introduces a family of methods called Knowledge-Graph Embedding-Based Attention (KGE-Attention), designed to enhance the performance of factual tasks like question answering (QA) and truth verification (TV). These approaches integrate a knowledge graph embedding (GIE) vector into traditional text-based attention mechanisms. We develop three distinct GIE vector types and combine each with two text-based vector representations to create a total of three novel frameworks. Extensive experiments conducted across two factual QA benchmarks and one TV benchmark demonstrate that our methods significantly outperform state-of-the-art techniques based on traditional text-based representations. Furthermore, our framework is versatile and can be easily adapted to any text-based factual task. Source code is accessible at https://github.com/PhucNguyen2001/KGE-Attention. Additionally, this work will be evaluated in the FLAIR factual QA challenge. Our findings indicate that utilizing knowledge graphs is an effective strategy for improving performance in factual-oriented tasks.

Optical tomograms provide a representative tool for visualizing nonclassical characteristics in the behavior of coherent states. While the transformation from quantum states to tomograms is typically linear, nonlinear effects usually vanish in the resulting optical transport diagrams. However, when two coherent states pass through a separable system of mirrors, beam spliders, and additional optical elements before entering a nonclassical beam splitter (NBCS), these nonlinear phenomena reappear within the combined optical tomograms at the output of the NBCS. These nonlinearity-induced phenomena highlight effects analogous to well-known nonclassical phenomena such as entanglement and quantum superposition. Specifically, we examine how nonlinearity manifests in optical tomograms as the transmissivity of the NBCS varies. Furthermore, we demonstrate how these nonlinear effects reveal the emergence of entanglement between two coherent states, a phenomenon that remains undetectable in traditional Wigner functions when the coherent state amplitude is large and the NBCS is nearly fully transmissive. Finally, we highlight a nonlinear manifestation of the swapping of entanglement between EPR correlations and bunching correlations as the transistentivity of the NBCS increases. The analysis presented here offers an intuitive method for visualizing nonclassical phenomena, particularly within the context of entanglement. Additionally, the technique can be extended to quantify nonclassical effects through an "optical entropy of entanglement." Such measurements are directly applicable to monitoring entanglement in squeezed vacuum states feeding the output ports of beam spliders, a crucial application for detecting gravitational wave nonclassicality. To facilitate these measurements, we propose the use of a "nonclassicality meter" based on time-dependent optical tomograms. This paper serves as an introductory guide to these concepts, making it suitable even for those new to the field. Ultimately, the connection between optical tomograms and the Wigner function is summarized, while the specifics of the nonclassicality meter are detailed in the sections that follow.
The study of charmed baryon decays has until now been limited to observing a single decay channel, $\Xi_c^0\to\Delta^{++-}\ell^+\nu_\ell$, with a measured branching fraction ranging from $1.9^{+1.5}_{-1.0}\times10^{-2}$ (statistical uncertainty only). Utilizing $1.5\,\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data collected at $\sqrt{s}=7\,\mathrm{TeV}$ by the LHCb experiment, we extend this analysis by first identifying seven additional decay modes and determining their relative branching fractions. We find that three potential fourth decay modes do not align with the signal region at greater than $2\sigma$ significance, with uncertainties dominated by systematic effects. No new fifth decay mode is identified. Employing isospin relations and the experimentally determined relative and absolute branching fractions for the five confirmed decay modes, we construct a phenomenological model to estimate the width of each mode and its associated uncertainties. These findings indicate that determining the absolute branching fractions for the four yet-undetected modes remains challenging due to large uncertainties. At the LHC, four of these missing modes are suppressed by phase space, while the fifth is hindered by a small hadronic form factor. Ultimately, at the High-Luminosity LHC, the number of observed decay modes will likely not substantially increase unless specific, theoretically motivated modes are theoretically calculated and prioritized for detection at the LHCb experiment.

This paper introduces a novel Lyapunov exponent defined within the cone of positive semidefinite matrices, offering a rigorous characterization of dynamical system stability. We establish that the new exponent is both necessary and sufficient for determining the long-term asymptotic stability of a specific mode. Furthermore, we derive a closed-form expression for this exponent and propose an efficient algorithm to calculate it. The advantages of our approach are highlighted through numerical examples. These benefits are additionalized to the description. Finally, the application of the new Lyapunov exponent is extended to analyze dynamical secrecy in the cone of positive semidefinite matrices.
This paper introduces the angle function for spaces that are not necessarily conformally embeddable into some $\R^n$, investigating how this function behaves under restricted geodesic variations. We define two novel concepts: almost nonnegative and nonnegative angle functions. It is well-established that a Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$ with a strictly nonnegative angle function and maximum dimension $n \ge 3$ can be conformally embedded into $\R^n$ preserving Riemannian metrics if and only if its angle function is strictly positive and satisfies the triangle inequality. Prior to this work, the nonnegative angle function was not formally defined for spaces outside of $\R^n$. Furthermore, we introduce the first example of a manifold with a nonnegative angle function that cannot be conformally embedded into any $\R^n$ to preserve its Riemannian metric. Finally, we examine the almost nonnegative angle function in the context of a rotationally symmetric surface with warping function $u(t)$, providing sufficient conditions for $(M,g)$ to be embeddable into $\R^3$. Our analysis reveals that for a surface of revolution, the conditions required to make the angle function nonnegative are significantly stronger than those needed to ensure the warping function is concave and has no inflection points.

This study introduces a novel Point Cloud Model certification method designed to assess certified accuracy when models are subjected to twisting transformations. We first present the Trecpc algorithm, a general framework applicable to various existing certified Point Neural Network (PNN) models. Subsequently, we detail the TPC framework, which enhances the Trecpc algorithm by integrating a new PNN correctness checker based on Sound Interval Arithmetic. This framework allows for the efficient optimization of correctness checker parameters during warm-up phases to achieve tighter tightness. Consequently, this results in higher certified accuracy against twisting transformations. Experimental results from hundreds of images generated via a Point Cloud conversion tool demonstrate that our Trecpc+ framework attested to significant improvements over six state-of-the-art PNN models, achieving three times greater certified accuracy for Nnvn, Inna, Fmax, and Fhn models, and five times more for the Stn model. To facilitate broader testing and evaluation, we have made the source code for the Trecpc and TPC methodologies available online at \url{https://github.com/yutao2015/TPC}.
We present a novel, fully automated algorithm for fallacious equation completion, integrated into a new error-localization environment called TELETUX. Programmers input an initial equation fragment, and the system suggests the most probable correct completion using our automated algorithm. Notably, TELETUX requires no labeled training data for either error localization or fallacious completion. The environment has been assessed using a large-scale dataset of incorrect equations from Wikibooks and Wikipedia. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that TELETUX achieves high accuracy in both error localization and suggesting corrected equations when evaluated on this real-world, noisy data. Furthermore, usability tests confirm that the environment is effective and that users are willing to adopt it within wiki communities to halt the spread of incorrect equations. To facilitate further research, we will openly release the eight gigabyte equity\_trace\_data set, the twenty gigabyte equity\_full_ set, and the TELETUX environment itself.

Self-sensing composite materials offer the potential for embedded damage detection through a self-sensing/self-healing architecture that integrates a piezoelectric patch for actuation and sensing with the composite itself. This study introduces a novel damage detection method rooted in signal processing and optimization theory. The approach combines an active sensing framework with a sensing image concept, utilizing Laser Interferometric Imaging (LII) as the reference standard for damage sensing. A genetic algorithm (GA) is employed to enhance the accuracy of damage detection from low-frequency sensing signals derived from piezoelectric outputs. By applying LII to create a known surface damage and then covering it with a piezoelectric sensing layer, a sensing signal is generated upon applying an electrical excitation and monitoring the response through a piezoelectric patch. The raw sensing signal is converted into a sensing vector, which is then mapped to amplitude-based features representing the composite's health state. These features are inputted into a GA-reconstructed composite imaging spectrum (RICIS) to reconstruct the damage image and estimate its dimensions. Experimental results from a nine-step process involving actual surface damage demonstrate that GA optimization significantly improves damage detection precision; specifically, a 50% reduction in excitation frequency from 900 Hz to 450 Hz, combined with signal processing and optimization, increased detection accuracy by 177%. Furthermore, the integration of optimization theory allowed for accurate damage image reconstruction and dimension estimation even after the excitation source was displaced by five millimeters. This cost-effective sensing and optimization framework holds promise for future composite material applications, particularly in aerospace engineering. Looking ahead, further research could explore the combined effects of multiple cracks and optimization theory, alongside the development of a piezoelectric imaging sensor capable of locating, measuring, and distinguishing between different types of damage.
This paper introduces a novel approach to deriving new integral identities by applying geometric vector methods within the fractional calculus domain. These vector techniques are used to transform existing fractional integral equations, thereby establishing various vector fractional integral relations that facilitate the creation of new fractional area- and solid-angle-related formulas. These formulations are then utilized to derive multiple fresh fractional integral identities, many of which appear to be original. The methodology is illustrated through several examples, and key fractional integral relations from recent literature are transformed via the geometric vector technique to establish additional new identities. Finally, the article concludes with a discussion on potential future research directions involving these geometric vector techniques in fractional calculus. The established new fractional integral identities have potential applications in physics, engineering, and related disciplines. Furthermore, these identities serve as a foundation for developing geometric operators and operators acting on function spaces, analogous to the impact of similar results in classical analysis.
This paper introduces the concept of $\Gamma$-actions on trees for right-angled Artin groups $A(\Gamma)$, associated with any subgraph $\Lambda$ of the defining graph $\Gamma$. We demonstrate that when $\Lambda$ is a subgraph of $\Gamma$ possessing non-empty complement and non-empty intersection, the corresponding $A(\Lambda)$-action on a tree admits a separating subgraph that is isomorphic to $\Lambda$. Furthermore, we establish that any two such actions on trees can be combined into a single $A(\Gamma)$-action on a tree through an amalgamated free product of the respective groups over their common stabilizing $A(\Lambda)$-subgraph actions. Finally, we prove the existence of a sequence of actions on trees for $A(\Gamma)$ that utilize completely disjoint subgraphs of $\Gamma$. As a consequence, we show that for any two non-trivial elements $g$ and $h$ in $A(\Gamma)$, there exists an $A(\Gamma)$-action on a tree where neither the stabilizer of an edge nor the stabilizer of the product of those edges in the boundary contains $g$ or $h$. Additionally, we derive that $A(\Gamma)$ satisfies the $Q$-Tits alternative for some integer $Q > 0$, implying a dichotomy: either $A(\Gamma)$ possesses $Q$ distinct actions on trees with no virtually stabilizing subgraph being cyclic, or it contains a non-trivial normal free abelian subgroup. As a corollary, we establish the existence of $Q$ distinct divisorial actions on the Gromov boundary. Concluding with the positive resolution to the Tits alternative, we show that $A(\Gamma)$ admits an action on a tree whose edge and product-of-edges stabilizers are virtually cyclic. Additionally, we prove the occurrence of linear divergence at infinity and the existence of a biLipschitz map from the Gromov boundary to a hyperbolic space. These findings collectively highlight the rich geometric structure inherent in $A(\Gamma)$.

This study addresses the challenge of function optimization for high-dimensional, nonconvex objectives through the Nested Minimax Descent (NMD) algorithm. While recent work by Agarwal et al. (2017) established linear convergence for the outer iterations of the Nested Neumann (NN) algorithm—relying on a limited number of nonnegative gradient components, termed "inception points"—the NN algorithm has historically suffered from a slow sublinear convergence rate for the inner iterations, hindered by the increasing inception depth. To mitigate this issue, we propose a modified variant of NMD that utilizes a fixed inception depth throughout the algorithm's execution. Our primary contribution is a proven linear convergence rate for the outer iterations that is independent of the inception depth. Additionally, we demonstrate that this new variant achieves a faster overall convergence rate for optimizing nonconvex functions compared to the traditional fixed-time-step NMD. Finally, numerical results indicate that the proposed variant converges more effectively than the uniform time-step NN algorithm in terms of reaching global stationary points for nonconvex functions. For deep nonconvex functions, our variant outperforms standard gradient descent methods. Our analysis does not depend on the dimensionality of the problem, and the number of iterations required for convergence is logarithmic regarding the proximity to global optimality. Furthermore, the linear convergence rate itself is logarithmic with respect to the log-distance from global optimality.
We introduce a novel approach to the contextual linear bandit problem that exploits the statistical properties of the context distribution. By incorporating a differentiable prior over the context distribution into the agent's state space, we achieve a significant reduction in the bits allocated for communication. This prior serves dual purposes: it guides the early-stage exploration of the state space and reduces the bit complexity required to describe the context throughout the learning process. Our algorithm, $\mathcal{A}_{\mathbf{b}}$, operates with $b$ bits per timesteps, utilizes $B$ total bits for learning the linear function, and has access to $\mathbf{b}$-bits of context information. For an horizon of $T$ timestep, the cumulative bit complexity amounts to $bT + B$. Assuming a bound of $N_T \leq (\log T)^{2}$ on the regret over $T$ timestep and defining $B = (\log T)^{3/2} (\mathbf{b} + b T)$, our analysis demonstrates that the expected linear regret over $T$ timestep does not exceed $c_1 \mathbf{b} \sqrt{T} + c_2 B + c_3 B \log (T/A_1)$ for some absolute constants $c_1, c_2, c_3 \geq 1$. Consequently, the per-timestep regret bounds scale as $O(\sqrt{T} + \log T)$. Furthermore, the agent requires only $b = O(\log T)$ bits per timestep, alongside an initial phase of $B$ timesteps dedicated to learning the linear component. In contrast to existing methods, our approach yields a nearly optimal bit complexity of $O(b T + T \log T)$ while maintaining regret bounds comparable to standard techniques. Additionally, the bit complexity per timestep remains independent of the total horizon $T$. Finally, we validate the efficacy of utilizing the context distribution's structure through numerical experiments. These tests compare the regret and exploration behavior of our method against a uniform baseline across various context distributions, highlighting superior performance with non-uniform distributions. Regarding the learning phase, our approach identifies the linear component with high precision using a $\log T$-factor fewer bits than uniform techniques, although it requires the distribution to be sufficiently structured to be represented within $B$ bits.

We present a collection of one-dimensional hydrodynamical disk models that incorporate heat transfer, cooling, radial dust advection, and stellar irradiation. Our primary objective is to assess the impact of outer-region dust growth on the thermal evolution and vertical stratification of protoplanetary disks. To achieve this, we developed a novel cooling function capable of accounting for varying dust opacity and efficiency across different optical depths and dust fractions. Our simulations indicate that in the outer regions, dust growth and increased opacity trap thermal radiation, thereby reducing cooling efficiency. This reduced efficiency is most pronounced in the low-density midplane where direct optical depths are minimal. Consequently, the presence of dust leads to higher midplane temperatures and increased gas pressure gradients, which in turn strengthen the hydrodynamical "convection" required to move material from the cooler, low-pressure surfaces toward the midplane. Regarding the settling of annular dust gaps, our results show that while higher dust fractions promote settling due to radial gradient forces, increased opacity and reduced cooling efficiency in the outer disk can counteract this, potentially leaving gaps more extended vertically. Overall, our findings suggest that purely hydrodynamical modeling may be insufficient for accurately simulating the evolution of large, outer-region dust gaps, as other physical processes could play a more significant role. To facilitate broader applications, we released an open-source Python script, \texttt{cooling.v1}, implementing our new cooling function for use with hydrodynamical disk models.
This paper establishes a new Liouville theorem for harmonic functions defined on gradient shrinking Ricci solitons that satisfy a novel growth restriction. By integrating this result with the work of Li and Tam, we derive a Liouville result on the same class of solitons for harmonic functions subject to the optimal growth condition identified by Yang and Xiao. Furthermore, utilizing the Liouville theorem concerning the prescribed mean curvature equation on gradient shrinking Ricci solitons within the optimal growth framework, we prove that all such solitons are isometric to the product manifold $\R\times\mathbb{M}^{n-1}$, where $\mathbb{M}^{n-1}$ represents a compact gradient shrinking Ricci soliton exhibiting optimal growth under its induced metric. Finally, we extend the initial growth constraint for harmonic functions for which a Liouville theorem has been proven on gradient shrinking Ricci solitons to the general manifold $M^n$. Our extended condition reads $|\nabla^{i}u| \le C r^{-(n-2)-\epsilon}$ for all $0\le i\le 2$, where $C$, $n$, and $\epsilon > 0$ are constants. Under this broader hypothesis, we derive an explicit formula for the Laplacian of the $q$-power mean $M_q(u)$, for which we also secure an upper bound; this bound relies on the structural constant $A$ associated with the soliton (as defined in \cite{HSY}), the geometric constant $K$ from the curvature bound $|\Rm| \le K$, and the structural constant $C$ from the intended growth condition. Consequently, under the curvature bound $|\Rm| \le K$, the soliton structural constant $A$, and the gradient bound $|\nabla u| \le D r^{-\gamma}$ (with $D>0$ and $0<\gamma<1$), we determine the optimal exponent $\alpha_{0}$ in the bound for $\Delta (u/e^{Ku})^{\alpha}$ that ensures the validity of this upper bound. Finally, we apply these findings to rederive the Liouville theorem for harmonic functions obeying the optimal growth condition on $|\nabla u|$.
Although deep neural networks are essential for automated decision-making, they remain susceptible to backdoor attacks, which can be triggered to produce specific unwanted outputs. While existing research predominantly focuses on implementing dynamic backdoors in convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for image classification—often relying on stealthy constructions like filter poisoning or feature mapping—these methods are computationally intensive and difficult to deploy in practice. This paper introduces a novel, lightweight dynamic backdoor mechanism capable of withstanding recent detection techniques. Although universal activation images are traditionally used, we demonstrate that backdoor attacks can be implemented dynamically without an image, simply by altering network parameters. Our analysis reveals that the concurrency of layers affected by the backdoor and the activation layer itself is critical for success; however, we can overcome this limitation using a matrix-based construction. This approach allows for the implementation of dynamic backdoors in any classification task, even those involving data with low dimensionality. Furthermore, we show that this method remains effective against recent detection schemes, including those designed for image classification. Finally, we validate the feasibility of this technique across multiple image and non-image datasets. To facilitate future research, we have open-sourced our framework at https://github.com/VincentYoo/TDB.

This paper examines the application of MM regularization within medical image segmentation, a common medical AI task. Moving beyond criticism, we identify the limitations of MM and propose two practical alternatives that require no extra computational resources. These new strategies significantly outperform MM, bringing performance closer to that of fully supervised approaches; indeed, one method sets a potential record for a single-source domain setting. These methods are easy to implement, demand no additional resources, and can be integrated into existing pipelines without modification. To their credit, this work demonstrates that MD regularization is not a failure but rather an area needing further refinement and research. Furthermore, we offer practical guidelines for researchers on how to apply interpolation mixing effectively. This study introduces a novel hybrid recurrent architecture, termed Factorized Dynamic-Static Long Short-Term Network (FDST-LSTM), designed to deliver high performance and energy efficiency for time-series workloads on constrained hardware platforms. Unlike conventional TDP-based hardware, the proposed FDHT-LSTM shares a single dynamic lookup table (LUT) across all hidden layers while utilizing distinct static LUTs for the first and subsequent layers. Furthermore, we integrate an FDST-LSTM structure with an LSTM-CNN model to maximize throughput and energy efficiency on resource-limited devices. Comparative analysis against state-of-the-art TDP-based hardware designs demonstrates that the FDST-LSTM achieves a 1.73x higher throughput and a 1.56x greater memory bandwidth. We are motivated to learn the structure of a binary function, which involves choosing the most plausible hypothesis based on a utility function that reflects our decision-driven reasons for learning. Although learning structure is inherently a Bayesian Bayesian optimization problem, existing literature has largely sidestepped explicitly defining the utility function. In this work, we fill that gap by introducing a logarithmic utility tailored to binary structure learning. We demonstrate that optimizing this utility is equivalent to maximizing the posterior probability of the hypothesis, an approach that also accommodates prior evidence about the structure. First, we provide theoretical bounds on the regret—defined as the difference between the actual utility and the optimal utility—considering a graph with $N$ nodes over $n$ iterations. These bounds indicate that $O(Nn \log n)$ iterations are required to achieve a regret no greater than zero. Second, we propose two iterative algorithms: one that guarantees a non-increasing utility at each step, and another that is guaranteed to increase the posterior probability of the structure. Finally, we present numerical results from a scenario with an unknown but sparse graph connecting two sensors, where our goal is to identify a spanning tree that minimizes total tracking latency. Our findings confirm that both proposed algorithms effectively learn the graph's structure within a short timeframe. Looking ahead, our framework of decision-making via a utility function for binary structure learning could be adapted to other structures, such as directed graphs. Furthermore, our regret analysis could be extended to consider multiple nodes, $N$, and time steps, $n$, and our optimization algorithm could be modified to address the combinatorial challenge of selecting $N-1$ edges among two nodes across numerous possible pairs.
This paper presents DiscSense, a comprehensive inventory of sense descriptions for discourse markers and their associated semantic relations. To address the lack of resources for documenting the semantic relationships between discourse markers and their constituent semantic relations (e.g., cause and effect), we developed a dataset comprising 3,333 distinct discourse markers annotated with context-free sense annotations (CSAs) and their corresponding relations. These annotations were curated using a subset of DiscWalli (Iwata et al., 2019) and the MultiVerses knowledge base (Touloupas et al., 2017). Finally, we constructed an API-enabled website offering access to this dataset. Accessible at https://dxn-lab.github.io/discsense/, the resource is designed to support downstream tasks such as discourse relation classification, discourse awareness machine reading questions (MRF-AI2), and the development of systems analyzing the cohesiveness of textual discourse. The dataset can be downloaded from https://osf.io/yz36w/download.

Regular expression containment represents a foundational challenge in the construction of regular expression trees, commonly known as "alpha folding." While Dessen and Poulin recently established the symbolic decidibility of regular expression containment using Brzozowski's operator— a decision symbol capable of eliminating one clause from sentences within a unidimensional Herbrand term algebra—extending this theory to decide containment between regular expressions adorned with predicates and quantifiers (complexy expressions) proves significantly more complex. This paper introduces a symbolic decision procedure for checking completeness, a task definition introduced by Serrano and Vianu. Unlike the approach for decidibility, our method for addressing completeness diverges from Brzozowski's operator; instead, we utilize a new operator that is at least as effective as the one used for decidibility. Furthermore, we adapt the procedure from decidibility, modifying it slightly to handle the problem of expression simplification. Although this might seem counterintuitive, as the team developing the compactness decision procedure typically develops a distinct simplification operator, our experience suggests that reusing the operator from the decidibility procedure (or the decidibility procedure itself) is often more efficient. Ultimately, our results indicate that a single decision operator is sufficient to tackle both the decidibility and compactness (decidibility) regular expression problems. Additionally, the unified procedure allows for the derivation of a polynomial bound N on the size of simplified expressions, enabling a explicit decision procedure based on tree searching beyond the bound N. However, deriving such a polynomial bound remains challenging and required specific assumptions regarding the expression alphabet and the distinction between predicate and function symbols. Finally, we outline how to adapt this decision procedure to decide the satisfiability of simple typed lambda calculus statements with identity and non-idempotent intersection types, a problem originally addressed by Serrano and Vianu via a different methodology.
